module: Drug dosing during Acute Kidney Injury and Renal Replacement Therapy

questions.question: Fluid overload in critically ill patients can lead to:
options: Decreased volume of distribution
Increased drug absorption
Sub-therapeutic plasma concentrations
Enhanced kidney metabolism
Enhanced liver metabolism
questions.explanation: Fluid overload dilutes the drug and increases the volume of distribution, especially for hydrophilic drugs, tending to produce sub-therapeutic plasma concentrations. Gut oedema can impair enteral absorption, and reduced renal and hepatic perfusion can impair organ metabolism, so the other options are incorrect.

questions.question: How is the clearance in continuous veno-venous hemodialysis (CVVHD) calculated?
options: Dialysate flow rate (Qd) multiplied by saturation coefficient (SA)
Effluent flow rate (Qeff) multiplied by sieving coefficient (SC)
Dialysate flow rate (Qd) multiplied by sieving coefficient (SC)
(Qeff + Qd) multiplied by saturation coefficient (SA)
Blood flow rate (Qb) divided by Dialysate flow rate (Qd) multiplied by saturation coefficient (SA)
questions.explanation: For CVVHD, drug clearance is estimated as dialysate flow rate multiplied by the saturation coefficient. Hemofiltration uses effluent flow times the sieving coefficient and hemodiafiltration sums both flows, so the other formulae describe different modalities.

questions.question: In the setting of intermittent forms of renal replacement therapy (RRT), which administration strategy is typically recommended for time-dependent antibiotics?
options: Administration before the RRT session
Continuous infusion during the RRT session
Administration after the RRT session
Intermittent infusion during the RRT session
Loading dose before the RRT session and top-up dose after the session
questions.explanation: For time-dependent antibiotics on intermittent RRT, giving the dose after the session preserves therapeutic concentrations, since dosing during dialysis risks removal and sub-therapeutic levels. Concentration-dependent agents may instead be given before the session so peaks can be cleared to limit toxicity.

questions.question: What is recommended to ensure optimal drug concentrations and safe therapy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury and those undergoing RRT?
options: Rely solely on initial dosing recommendations from published references
Disregard pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics when adjusting doses
Utilise regular monitoring and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)
Avoid reassessing drug doses due to the dynamic nature of acute kidney injury
Reduce the loading dose for all drugs in patients with AKI and those undergoing RRT to minimise the risk of toxicity
questions.explanation: Because pharmacokinetics are highly variable in AKI and RRT, regular reassessment with therapeutic drug monitoring best ensures effective and safe concentrations. Relying solely on published tables, ignoring pharmacokinetics, or refusing to reassess would all risk mis-dosing.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of solute and drug removal in continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVH)?
options: Diffusion
Convection
Osmosis
Active transport
Adsorption
questions.explanation: Hemofiltration removes solutes and drugs primarily by convection driven by a pressure gradient, which also clears larger molecules. Diffusion is the main mechanism in haemodialysis, while osmosis, active transport and adsorption are not the relevant mechanisms in CRRT.

questions.question: Which of the following factors does not affect drug clearance in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI)?
options: Hypoalbuminemia
Change in protein binding
Type of renal replacement therapy
Endogenous kidney function
Mode of action of the drug
questions.explanation: A drug's mode of action does not determine how it is cleared. Hypoalbuminaemia and altered protein binding change the volume of distribution, and the renal replacement modality and any residual kidney function all affect clearance.

questions.question: Which of the following methods is considered the most accurate surrogate measure of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in critically ill patients?
options: Cockcroft-Gault equation
Modified Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) equation
Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation
Measured creatinine clearance using the UV/P formula
Urea-Creatinine Ratio
questions.explanation: A measured creatinine clearance using the UV/P formula is the most accurate bedside surrogate of GFR in the critically ill, as the estimating equations were not validated in AKI. The urea-to-creatinine ratio may suggest the cause of renal failure but does not measure GFR.

questions.question: Why does dosing of drugs in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) and those undergoing renal replacement therapies (RRT) pose a challenge?
options: Because pharmacokinetics do not change during AKI or RRT
Because traditional methods of evaluating glomerular filtration rate (GFR) become more reliable during RRT
Because initial dosing recommendations apply primarily to patients with AKI
Because of the unpredictable and highly variable changes in drug pharmacokinetics
Because guidance on drug dosing from the product license is based on phase 4 post marketing studies in a wide range of patients including critically ill patient who require RRT
questions.explanation: Dosing is difficult because pharmacokinetics in AKI and RRT are unpredictable and highly variable. Traditional GFR estimates become unreliable on RRT, and product-label guidance derives from studies in stable patients, so it cannot be assumed to apply.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding renal replacement therapies (RRT) in the ICU are true?

statements.label: A
statements.text: RRT techniques primarily focus on compensating for processes of secretion and metabolism

statements.label: B
statements.text: Intermittent haemodialysis (IHD) relies on convection for solute removal

statements.label: C
statements.text: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is administered over short periods, typically 4-6 hours

statements.label: D
statements.text: The prescribed clearance for CRRT is often overestimated compared to the actual delivered clearance

questions.explanation: Renal replacement primarily compensates for clearance and excretion, not secretion and metabolism, so that statement is false. Intermittent haemodialysis relies on diffusion rather than convection, and continuous therapy runs over roughly 24 hours rather than a few hours; only the point that prescribed CRRT clearance often exceeds the delivered clearance is true.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding antibiotic dosing in critically ill patients with AKI or undergoing RRT is true?

statements.label: A
statements.text: Serum creatinine is a reliable marker for adjusting antibiotic doses during RRT

statements.label: B
statements.text: Antibiotic therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is not recommended in cases of AKI or RRT

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dose reductions of renally eliminated antibiotics should be avoided during the first 24 hours of sepsis or septic shock

statements.label: D
statements.text: PK alterations in antibiotic dosing are static processes and do not require regular re-evaluation

questions.explanation: In early sepsis or septic shock the volume of distribution is often increased, so dose reductions of renally-eliminated antibiotics should be avoided, which makes that statement true. Serum creatinine is not reliable on RRT, therapeutic drug monitoring is recommended, and pharmacokinetic changes are dynamic and need regular review.
